fields.h1: The Fourfold Gospel by A. B. Simpson: A Study Guide
fields.meta_title: The Fourfold Gospel by A. B. Simpson — Summary & Study Guide
fields.description: A reader’s study guide to A. B. Simpson’s The Fourfold Gospel — Christ our Saviour, Sanctifier, Healer, and Coming King. Summary, key themes, who should read it, and reflection questions, with the full free text on Ochorus.
fields.body_html:
Few phrases in modern Christian history have carried as much weight in so few words as A. B. Simpson’s “fourfold gospel.” It is his shorthand for a whole Christ met at four points of human need: Christ our Saviour, our Sanctifier, our Healer, and our Coming King. This study guide walks through The Fourfold Gospel — free to read in full on Ochorus — so that you can grasp Simpson’s argument quickly, read the book with more understanding, and see why this small volume shaped a worldwide movement. If you want the short answer to “what is the fourfold gospel?”, it is this: not four blessings to collect, but one Person to receive.

What the book is, and Simpson’s “fourfold gospel” framework

The Fourfold Gospel is a compact set of chapters, drawn from the preaching of A. B. Simpson (1843–1919), the Canadian-born pastor who founded the Christian and Missionary Alliance and built the first Bible college in North America. Where many books labour a single theme, Simpson sets out to sketch the fullness of what Christ is to a believer, and he does it in four movements that he insists are one.

The framework is deceptively simple. Simpson takes the human predicament — guilt, an unholy heart, a failing body, and a groaning world — and answers each with a facet of Christ. To the guilty he offers the Saviour; to the divided heart, the Sanctifier; to the suffering body, the Healer; to the weary and watching, the Coming King. The genius of the scheme is that it refuses to let any one of these swallow the others. Simpson had lived long enough in revival circles to see people chase an experience — a feeling, a gift, a healing — and mistake it for the whole. His whole aim is to point past the gift to the Giver.

That instinct became the confession of his life, and he set it to verse in his hymn “Himself”: once it was the blessing, now it is the Lord. The Fourfold Gospel is that hymn turned into teaching. Read it as one portrait in four panels, not four unrelated doctrines.

The four aspects of the one Christ

Simpson takes the folds in a deliberate order, each resting on the one before. It is worth following him panel by panel.

Christ our Saviour

The book opens where the gospel opens, with salvation — and, strikingly, with a scene from the very end of the story. Simpson takes his text from Revelation 7:10, the cry of the ransomed around the throne: salvation belongs to God and to the Lamb. He wants the reader to feel salvation not as a transaction filed away at conversion but as the song of a rescued people who look back over “the toils they have come through and the perils they have escaped.” Christ is first of all the One who saves — freely, fully, and forever. Everything else in the book is built on this floor and never leaves it.

Christ our Sanctifier

The second fold is the one Simpson labours most, because it is the one most easily confused. Sanctification, he says, is not regeneration; it is not the same as becoming a Christian, precious as that is. Taking his text from John 17:19 — Christ sanctifying Himself for His people’s sake — Simpson argues that holiness is not the believer’s achievement but Christ’s own life imparted, a Person received rather than a standard struggled toward. His most memorable image draws the line exactly:

Regeneration is like building a house and having the work done well. Sanctification is having the owner come and dwell in it and fill it with gladness, and life, and beauty.

A. B. Simpson

Here is the heart of Simpson’s deeper-life teaching. Many Christians, he warns, are converted and stop there. The invitation of this chapter is to let the Owner move in.

Christ our Healer

The third fold was the most controversial in Simpson’s day and remains the one readers wrestle with most. His texts are Matthew 8:17 — “Himself took our infirmities and bare our sicknesses” — and Hebrews 13:8, that Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever. Simpson roots healing in the atonement, tying it to Isaiah 53:4, and insists it is the work of God rather than of medicine:

It is the direct power of the Almighty hand of God Himself.

A. B. Simpson

Notably, Simpson is not reckless. He allows that those who cannot yet trust their bodies wholly to the Lord may rightly use “all the help that nature and science can give,” and he warns against giving up human helps rashly before one has found “a better one.” He presents divine healing soberly, as one fold of the full gospel and never a novelty to be paraded.

Christ our Coming King

The fourth fold crowns the rest. From Revelation 2:28 — “I will give him the morning star” — Simpson presents the return of Christ as “the glorious culmination of all other parts of the Gospel.” Salvation, he notes, is “ready to be revealed in the last time”; sanctification finds its end when, as 1 John 3:2 says, “we shall be like Him”; and healing is only “the first-springing life of which the resurrection will be the full fruition.” So the folds converge:

So that the truth and hope of the Lord’s coming is linked with all truth and life, and is the Church’s great and blessed hope.

A. B. Simpson

The book’s later chapters — on “The Walk with God” (from 1 John 2:6) and on being “Kept” (from 2 Timothy 1:12 and 1 Peter 1:5) — apply the fourfold Christ to daily discipleship: a life that walks as He walked, and a soul garrisoned by the power of God.

Central themes to watch for

Several threads run through every chapter and are worth tracing as you read.

A whole Christ for the whole person. Simpson refuses to divide the human being into a soul the gospel cares about and a body it does not. Guilt, holiness, health, and hope are all met in one Christ. This unity is the book’s deepest claim.

The Giver, not the gift. Again and again Simpson redirects the reader from the experience to the Person who gives it. Healing meetings at his own church, he was careful to say, were hours of worship before they were anything else. Watch how he steers every blessing back to Christ Himself.

Received by faith, not achieved by effort. Whether it is sanctification, healing, or being kept, Simpson’s verbs are receiving, trusting, and abiding. The Christian life he describes is one of dependence, not strain — a house indwelt rather than a project completed.

Hope that sanctifies. The forward tilt toward Christ’s return is not escapism; for Simpson it purifies present living and fuels mission. The blessed hope is a spur, not a sedative.

Who should read it — and a fair word on the healing strand

The Fourfold Gospel rewards almost any reader who wants to move beyond a partial gospel into the fullness of Christ. New believers will find a clear map of what Christ offers; longtime Christians who have settled into forgiveness without pressing on to sanctification will find a gentle, urgent nudge forward. Pastors and teachers will find a model of how to hold together truths that are often set against one another. And anyone curious about the roots of the deeper-life and Alliance movements will find their headwaters here.

One honest note. The third fold — divine healing — is where thoughtful Christians differ, and it is fair to say so plainly. Simpson taught that bodily healing is part of the atonement and available to faith now; other equally serious believers hold that while God still heals, the New Testament does not promise healing to all in this age, and that suffering can be God’s sanctifying gift. This guide presents Simpson’s view as his, argued from his texts, not as the settled position of the whole church. Read the healing chapter as you would any strong argument: weigh it against Scripture, notice Simpson’s own sobriety about medicine, and hold the point charitably. The other three folds stand regardless of where you land on this one.

How to read it today

Take the folds in Simpson’s own order — Saviour, Sanctifier, Healer, Coming King — because each builds on the last into a single portrait. The book is short enough to read straight through in a couple of sittings, and it rewards that, since the cumulative effect is the whole Christ Simpson means to present.

Keep a Bible open beside it. Every chapter hangs on a text, and Simpson expects you to be reading with him; look up Revelation 7:10, John 17:19, Matthew 8:17, and Revelation 2:28 in your own translation before you read his exposition of each. Simpson wrote in the cadence of the King James Version, so give the older English a moment to settle; the thought underneath is warm and plain.

Then let it lead you further into Simpson. His daily devotional, Days of Heaven Upon Earth, distils the same message into a reading for every day of the year, and is the natural companion once the framework of the fourfold gospel is in your hands. Read the doctrine here, then live in it there.

For reflection

Use these questions on your own or with a group, one per chapter or all at once.

  • Simpson says many Christians are “converted and stop there.” In your own life, which of the four folds have you received, and which have you left unopened?
  • What is the practical difference between building the house well (regeneration) and letting the Owner move in (sanctification)? Where would others see that difference in you?
  • How do you weigh Simpson’s teaching on healing against your own reading of Scripture and your own experience of suffering? What can you receive from him even if you differ?
  • Simpson calls Christ’s return “the Church’s great and blessed hope.” Does that hope actually shape how you live this week — or has it become a doctrine you affirm but rarely feel?
  • Simpson’s whole aim is to move you from the blessing to the Blesser. Where are you tempted to want the gift more than the Giver, and what would it look like to seek Christ Himself?
